label: Reliance on chance variation and natural selection stalls inquiry into physical causes
claim: As long as fortuitous variation and the survival of the fittest are accepted as sufficient explanations in biology, they will tend to hold back careful investigation of the real physical causes of organic form.
quote: So long and so far as “fortuitous variation” and the “survival of the fittest” remain engrained as fundamental and satisfactory hypotheses in the philosophy of biology, so long will these “satisfactory and specious causes” tend to stay “severe and diligent inquiry,”
scope: explanations of organic form in biology generally
candidate_data: none known

label: Cells, tissues, shells, bones, leaves and flowers are shaped by the laws of physics
claim: The material parts of living things (cells, tissues, shells, bones, leaves, flowers) are portions of matter whose particles have been moved, moulded and shaped in obedience to the laws of physics.
quote: Cell and tissue, shell and bone, leaf and flower, are so many portions of matter, and it is in obedience to the laws of physics that their particles have been moved, moulded and conformed.
scope: all organisms and their structural parts
measurable_quantities: mechanical stresses and surface tensions in tissues
candidate_data: Cell and tissue shape imaging datasets (Allen Cell Explorer, Image Data Resource) paired with published tissue mechanics measurements; 3D morphology scans in MorphoSource.

label: Problems of organic form are mathematical and problems of growth are physical
claim: The problems of the form of living things are, in the first instance, mathematical problems and their problems of growth are essentially physical problems, so morphology is a branch of physical science.
quote: Their problems of form are in the first instance mathematical problems, and their problems of growth are essentially physical problems; and the morphologist is, _ipso facto_, a student of physical science.
scope: morphology and the study of growth
candidate_data: none known

label: No known physical law is transgressed by the bodily mechanism
claim: However complex living processes are, no physical law (including those of chemistry, surface action and osmosis) is known to be broken by the working of the body.
quote: But all the while, so far as I am aware, no physical law, any more than that of gravity itself, not even among the puzzles of chemical “stereometry,” or of physiological “surface-action” or “osmosis,” is known to be _transgressed_ by the bodily mechanism.
scope: the physical and physiological mechanisms of all organisms
measurable_quantities: energy and mass balance of organisms
osmotic and surface forces in tissues
candidate_data: Whole-organism calorimetry and energy-balance studies and published physiological measurements of osmosis and membrane transport.

section: Form as a diagram of forces
label: The form of an object is a diagram of the forces acting or that have acted on it
claim: The form of any portion of matter, living or dead, can be read as a diagram of forces: from the shape of a solid one can deduce the forces that produced and maintain it, and from the shape of a fluid the forces currently acting on it, so an organism's conformation is explained by a balance of forces.
quote: In short, the form of an object is a “diagram of forces,” in this sense, at least, that from it we can judge of or deduce the forces that are acting or have acted upon it
scope: living and non-living bodies, including whole organisms and cells
measurable_quantities: shape of cells or skeletal elements
measured or inferred mechanical stresses and forces
candidate_data: Studies inferring cell and tissue forces from shape (cell-shape image datasets such as the Image Data Resource) and finite-element analyses of bone built on MorphoSource scans.

label: Protoplasm behaves as a highly viscous fluid that changes shape under force
claim: The protoplasm of an Amoeba deforms and flows under the slightest pressure, so it is a fluid, but it is far more viscous than water, like treacle, and this viscosity slows its changes of shape.
quote: While the protoplasm of the Amoeba reacts to the slightest pressure, and tends to “flow,” and while we therefore speak of it as a fluid, it is evidently far less mobile than such a fluid, for instance, as water, but is rather like treacle in its slow creeping movements as it changes its shape in response to force.
scope: protoplasm of Amoeba and similar naked cells
candidate_data: Published microrheology and micropipette-aspiration measurements of cytoplasmic viscosity in amoebae and other cells.

label: Surface tension at a cell's boundary strongly affects its form
claim: Like other fluid bodies, the surface of a cell such as an Amoeba carries a surface tension that depends on the substance it touches, and this surface tension strongly affects the cell's form.
quote: Like other fluid bodies, its surface, whatsoever other substance, gas, liquid or solid, it be in contact with, and in varying degree according to the nature of that adjacent substance, is the seat of molecular force exhibiting itself as a surface-tension, from the action of which many important consequences follow, which greatly affect the form of the fluid surface.
scope: fluid or semi-fluid cells such as Amoeba
candidate_data: Published micropipette and atomic-force-microscopy measurements of cell cortical tension alongside cell-shape images (Image Data Resource).

label: Vital phenomena cannot be cleanly divided into physical and non-physical ones
claim: There is no clear rule for deciding what is 'vital', and the properties of organisms cannot be clearly split into those of physical origin and those peculiar to living things, so physical analysis must proceed piece by piece.
quote: it is plain that we have no clear rule or guide as to what is “vital” and what is not; the whole assemblage of so-called vital phenomena, or properties of the organism, cannot be clearly classified into those that are physical in origin and those that are _sui generis_ and peculiar to living things.
scope: properties and processes of living organisms
candidate_data: none known

label: Nuclei, chromosomes and germ-plasm act only as seats of energy and centres of force
claim: In development, variation and inheritance, material elements such as the spermatozoon, nucleus, chromosomes or germ-plasm never act as matter alone, but only as seats of energy and centres of force.
quote: we must most carefully realise in the outset that the spermatozoon, the nucleus, the chromosomes or the germ-plasm can never _act_ as matter alone, but only as seats of energy and as centres of force.
scope: embryology and heredity
candidate_data: none known

label: Changes in the length-weight constant k reveal changes of form during growth
claim: Weight varies as the cube of length (W = kL³) in an animal of unchanging form and density, so tracking whether k stays constant or varies with length shows whether the animal's general form changes as it grows; such changes are likely as long as growth continues.
quote: then the value of _k_, according to whether it varies or remains constant, will tell us at once whether there has or has not been a tendency to gradual alteration in the general form.
scope: fishes and other growing animals of roughly constant density
candidate_data: Length-weight relationship parameters compiled in FishBase and fisheries survey length-weight records.

label: Gravity sets an upper limit on the size of terrestrial animals
claim: Because the strength of muscles and the crushing resistance of bones vary as their cross-section (the square of linear size) while body weight varies as the cube, there is a definite upper limit to the size of an animal living under gravity; the elephant, with disproportionately thick limb bones and reduced agility, is already near it.
quote: But in a terrestrial animal the weight which tends to crush its limbs or which its muscles have to move, varies as the cube of its linear dimensions; and so, to the possible magnitude of an animal, living under the direct action of gravity, there is a definite limit set.
scope: terrestrial animals, especially large mammals
candidate_data: Published compilations of limb-bone circumference and body mass across mammals, 3D bone scans in MorphoSource, and body masses from PanTHERIA.

label: Buoyancy removes the physical barrier to size in fully aquatic animals
claim: An animal wholly immersed in water whose density about matches the water, like a whale, has its weight counterpoised, so there is no longer a physical barrier to its indefinite growth in size.
quote: Under these circumstances there is no longer a physical barrier to the indefinite growth in magnitude of the animal.
scope: fully aquatic animals of near-neutral buoyancy, e.g. whales
measurable_quantities: maximum body mass of aquatic versus terrestrial lineages
candidate_data: Body-mass compilations for mammals (PanTHERIA) and fossil body-size records in the Paleobiology Database comparing aquatic and terrestrial maxima.

label: Tree trunk diameter must grow as the 3/2 power of height
claim: For a tree to stand without buckling under its own weight, its diameter must increase as the 3/2 power of its height, which explains why young trees are slender and old large ones stunted, and sets a theoretical maximum tree height (about 300 ft for a Kew-flagstaff pine).
quote: In general, as Greenhill shews, the diameter of a homogeneous body must increase as the power 3/2 of the height, which accounts for the slender proportions of young trees, compared with the stunted appearance of old and large ones.
scope: trees and other tall self-supporting plant stems
candidate_data: Tree height-diameter allometry databases such as Tallo, national forest inventory data, and TRY plant traits for wood density and maximum height.

label: Larger fish can sprint faster but cover similar distances and tire more slowly
claim: Since muscular work available scales as the cube of linear size while the rate of energy supply, depending on respiratory surface, scales only as the square, a larger fish should achieve a much higher burst speed than a smaller one but travel a similar distance over a year, and smaller individuals should fatigue faster and have less staying power.
quote: the singular result ought to follow that, in swimming for instance, the larger fish ought to be able to put on a spurt of speed far in excess of the smaller one; but the distance travelled by the year’s end should be very much alike for both of them.
scope: similar, closely related animals of different size, especially swimming fish
candidate_data: Published swimming-performance datasets (burst and critical swimming speeds), animal telemetry tracking records, and metabolic-rate data in AnAge and AnimalTraits.

label: Power needed for flight grows as length^3.5 while muscle power grows as length^3
claim: A bird of fixed proportions must fly at a minimum speed proportional to the square root of its linear size, so the work needed for flight varies as the 3½ power of linear size while the work its muscles can supply varies only as the cube; flight thus becomes harder as birds get larger (about 1.4 times harder per doubling of length).
quote: The work requiring to be done, then, varies as the power 3½ of the bird’s linear dimensions, while the work of which the bird is capable depends on the mass of its muscles, and therefore varies as the cube of its linear dimensions.
scope: flying birds of similar proportions
candidate_data: Published bird flight-speed measurements (e.g. radar and tracking studies), flight-muscle mass compilations, and body masses from AnimalTraits.

label: Ostrich and moa have passed the size at which muscular flight is possible
claim: The ostrich probably, and the moa certainly, reached a size at which flight by muscular action with ordinary bird anatomy became physiologically impossible, and a bird as large as a man could not fly.
quote: It is not improbable that the ostrich has already reached a magnitude, and we may take it for certain that the moa did so, at which flight by muscular action, according to the normal anatomy of a bird, has become physiologically impossible.
scope: large birds, including ratites
candidate_data: Body-mass compilations of extant and extinct birds (AnimalTraits; Paleobiology Database for fossil taxa) with flight ability recorded.

section: Giant fossil fliers and air density
label: Giant Carboniferous insects and pterodactyls imply a denser ancient atmosphere
claim: The giant wingspans of Carboniferous dragonflies and the small bodies and huge wings of pterodactyls, which seem beyond present mechanical limits, can be explained if the Carboniferous and Jurassic atmosphere was notably denser, for example through more carbonic acid.
quote: we have only to suppose that in carboniferous and jurassic days the terrestrial atmosphere was notably denser than it is at present, by reason, for instance, of its containing a much larger proportion of carbonic acid, and we have at once a means of reconciling the apparent mechanical discrepancy.
scope: Carboniferous giant insects and Jurassic pterosaurs
measurable_quantities: reconstructed atmospheric density or composition through time
candidate_data: Fossil insect and pterosaur size records in the Paleobiology Database and published geochemical reconstructions of Phanerozoic atmospheric CO2 and O2.

label: Similarly built animals should jump to the same absolute height regardless of size
claim: Because the impulse of a leap is proportional to muscle volume and so to body mass, the take-off velocity is independent of size, and similarly built animals should jump to the same actual height rather than the same relative height; longer levers in larger animals give them some advantage.
quote: in other words, that all animals, provided always that they are similarly fashioned, with their various levers etc., in like proportion, ought to jump, not to the same relative, but to the same actual height.
scope: jumping animals of similar construction across sizes, from fleas to horses
candidate_data: Published comparative jumping-performance datasets across insects, frogs and mammals with body mass.

label: Speed varies as the square root of linear size in swimming, flight and walking
claim: Leaving aside differences in mechanical construction, swimming (Froude's law), flight (minimum stable speed) and walking (the leg swinging as a pendulum) all give the same result: an animal's velocity tends to vary as the square root of its linear dimensions.
quote: the general result, attained under very different conditions and arrived at by very different modes of reasoning, is in every case that the velocity tends to vary as the square root of the linear dimensions of the organism.
scope: swimming, flying and walking animals of similar construction
candidate_data: Published compilations of maximum and preferred locomotor speeds against body size for fish, birds and mammals, with body sizes from AnimalTraits or PanTHERIA.

label: Doubling gravity would make terrestrial animals short-legged or serpent-like
claim: The form and actions of terrestrial animals are conditioned by the strength of gravity: if it were doubled, bipedal form would fail and most land animals would resemble short-legged saurians or serpents; if halved, animals would be lighter, more active and need less heart, lungs and blood.
quote: Were the force of gravity to be doubled, our bipedal form would be a failure, and the majority of terrestrial animals would resemble short-legged saurians, or else serpents.
scope: terrestrial animals
measurable_quantities: skeletal and cardiovascular measures under altered gravity
candidate_data: Published hypergravity centrifuge and spaceflight studies of animal morphology and physiology.

label: Folded surfaces such as villi and brain convolutions keep surface in step with mass
claim: Throughout morphology, surface tends to keep pace with volume through changes of form, such as intestinal villi and folds, the shark's spiral valve, and brain convolutions whose complexity is correlated with animal size, so that a roughly constant ratio of surface to mass is maintained.
quote: Throughout the whole field of morphology we may find examples of a tendency (referable doubtless in each case to some definite physical cause) for surface to keep pace with volume, through some alteration of its form.
scope: internal surfaces of animals, e.g. gut lining and brain cortex
measurable_quantities: cortical surface area or gyrification index
candidate_data: Published comparative datasets of brain gyrification and cortical surface area across mammals and of intestinal surface area against body mass.

label: Form of small organisms is set by surface tension, not gravity, favouring spheres
claim: The form of all small organisms is largely independent of gravity and mainly due to surface tension, acting either now or at an earlier stage before the form was made rigid, so small organisms tend strongly toward spherical and other simple surface-tension forms that do not occur in the external form of large animals.
quote: In like manner we shall find that the form of all small organisms is largely independent of gravity, and largely if not mainly due to the force of surface-tension
scope: small organisms and individual cells versus large animals
measurable_quantities: shape sphericity or other shape descriptors
candidate_data: Plankton and protist imaging datasets with size and shape measurements, and cell-shape data in the Image Data Resource.

label: Form follows growth rates in large organisms but not in minute ones
claim: Large and small organisms differ in kind in how form arises: in large organisms form is the direct result of unequal growth rates in different directions, but in minute organisms and individual cells intermolecular forces outweigh gravity and form is not simply correlated with growth.
quote: But it is by no means true that form and growth are in this direct and simple fashion correlative or complementary in the case of minute portions of living matter.
scope: large multicellular organisms versus small organisms and individual cells
candidate_data: Time-lapse growth and morphometric datasets of developing organisms and of single cells (Image Data Resource).

label: Cell division restores the ratio of surface to mass
claim: Cell division keeps the ratio between a cell's surface and its mass approximately constant and restores the balance of surface energy with the cell's other energies; cleavage of an egg increases surface without increasing volume or mass.
quote: In short, however it may be brought about, the phenomenon of division of the cell will be precisely what is required to keep approximately constant the ratio between surface and mass, and to restore the balance between the surface-energy and the other energies of the system.
scope: dividing cells, including cleaving eggs
candidate_data: Cell-size and cell-cycle imaging datasets (Allen Cell Explorer, Image Data Resource) and published embryo cleavage volume measurements.

label: Cells of each kind vary little about a mean size, whatever the body size
claim: Cells of each kind vary little about a characteristic mean size and have absolute size limits, so dwarf and giant individuals of a species (e.g. Crepidula, sea-urchin larvae) differ in cell number rather than cell size.
quote: An immediate and remarkable result of the principles just described is a tendency on the part of all cells, according to their kind, to vary but little about a certain mean size, and to have, in fact, certain absolute limitations of magnitude.
scope: tissue cells of animals, compared across individuals of different body size
candidate_data: Published cell-size measurements across body sizes within and between species, and tissue histology images in the Image Data Resource.

label: Ganglion-cell size varies little; larger species have ganglia with more cells
claim: Across animals large and small, ganglion (nerve) cells vary in size only within narrow limits, and smaller species have simpler ganglia containing fewer cells than larger species.
quote: we may (with Enriques) lay it down as a general law that among animals, whether large or small, the ganglion-cells vary in size within narrow limits; and that, amidst all the great variety of structural type of ganglion observed in different classes of animals, it is always found that the smaller species have simpler ganglia than the larger, that is to say ganglia containing a smaller number of cellular elements.
scope: nerve cells and ganglia across animal species
measurable_quantities: neuron number per ganglion or brain region
candidate_data: Published comparative neuron-count datasets (isotropic fractionator studies across mammals and birds) and NeuroMorpho.Org neuron morphologies.

label: The smallest organisms approach molecular size, so they cannot be much smaller
claim: Because a micrococcus 0.15 µm across contains only some tens of thousands of protein molecules, the smallest known organisms approach molecular dimensions, and organisms cannot be subdivided indefinitely or be much smaller than those already discovered.
quote: it will still be clear that the smallest known bodies which are described as organisms draw nigh towards molecular magnitudes, and we must recognise that the subdivision of the organism cannot proceed to an indefinite extent, and in all probability cannot go very much further than it appears to have done in these already discovered forms.
scope: the smallest micro-organisms
measurable_quantities: number of protein molecules per cell
candidate_data: Published cell-size measurements of the smallest bacteria and archaea, and proteomic estimates of protein copy number per cell.
